Mendacious

/men-DAY-shuhs/ - the stress falls on DAY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mendacious means deliberately untruthful; lying.

Fact-checkers counted eleven mendacious claims in the celebrity's twelve-minute interview.

Worked Example

The 'haunted lighthouse' pamphlet sold in the gift shop is cheerfully mendacious: the keeper it mourns never existed, the shipwreck it describes happened in another country, and the 'original logbook' on display was printed the year the shop opened.

Mendacious is stronger than 'misleading' because it accuses the source of deliberate lies, not sloppy errors—a mistaken guide gets the facts wrong; a mendacious one invents them on purpose.

How Mendacious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

deceitful

deceitful: practicing deception of any kind, in word or act; mendacious lies in words

untruthful

untruthful: the mild, careful way to say the same thing

Antonyms

truthful

truthful: telling things as they are

honest

honest: upright in word and dealing alike

How Strong Is It? — mistaken → misleading → mendacious

mistaken vs. mendacious

mistaken vs. mendacious: Mistaken stops far short of mendacious — a mistaken witness is wrong without meaning to be.

misleading vs. mendacious

misleading vs. mendacious: Misleading stops short of mendacious — a misleading claim bends true facts, while a mendacious one invents them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mendaci-

Root — mendaci-: lying (Latin mendax, from menda, a fault)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Mendaci- (lying) + -ous = full of lies. Latin mendax, 'a liar,' grew from menda, 'a fault or blemish' — as though every lie were a flaw pressed into the record. A mendacious report is one whose faults were put there on purpose.

Use the root in a new word: mendacity

Use the root in a new word: mendacity: The editorial accused the ministry of plain mendacity about the dam's true costs.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / accusatory

Mendacious is a formal accusation of deliberate lying — auditors, historians, and editorials use it when 'inaccurate' would be too kind. Its unit-mate perfidious accuses something different: the mendacious lie in what they say, while the perfidious betray a trust they still pretend to keep.
